## TL;DR

Worktree cleanup is now automatic and fail-closed. One shared sweep reclaims
only worktrees RepoOS can prove redundant with main, reports every retained
entry with an actionable reason, and lists worktrees outside its managed
directory as external and untouched. The 2026-11-02 audit found no remaining
provable candidates, so the live residue is correctly retained. On the final
tree I re-ran the scoped gate with `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main`: every executed
step passed, including the full build, UI smoke, rendered contrast audit and
user-docs build, and the three changed test files passed locally (89 tests).
The earlier handoff failures were report length and a stale partial docs build,
not code.

## Work and rationale

`sweepStaleWorktrees` is the single policy shared by boot, close-out,
`repoos gc`, `gc --dry-run`, and `repoos status`, so candidate, retained and
external counts cannot drift; tests assert that agreement.

Eligibility is proven, never inferred from metadata. A task is resolved only
when it is `done`, or archived **and** AI-assigned; archived-but-ready and
human-assigned tasks stay retained. For a resolved task the sweep tries
ancestry, then a content proof that compares the branch tip against main over
the paths the branch touched. A recorded `merged_commit` skips already-shipped
commits, so WIP checkpoints are reclaimable. Non-ancestor branches proven by
content delete with `-D`; dry-run reports the same deletion.

Dirty `work/*.md` files do not block cleanup by path alone: each is compared
byte-for-byte with main's canonical copy and reclaimed only on an exact match or
deletion; unique task data retains the worktree. Tests cover unique
noncanonical task content explicitly.

Ignored files need explicit handling because `git status` hides them. A
worktree holding a local `.env`, attachment tree, or scratch data is retained;
only a scoped allowlist of regenerable output (root `dist`/`coverage`/cache,
`node_modules`, VitePress builds) may be discarded. An inherited `.env` symlink
into the canonical checkout is the one safe exception; an unresolvable symlink
is an inspection failure that retains.

## Approaches tried

The early sweep was integrate-only, which let the 2026-11-01 residue
accumulate. I replaced it with a full safe sweep gated on the task index and
durable close-out records; unreadable state skips cleanup rather than treating
everything as inactive. A path-shape check for ignored output was too broad:
review showed nested `dist`/`coverage`/`.repoos` could be tracked source, so it
now targets exact root locations.

## Challenges and blockers

The hard part was distinguishing "provably absent" from "could not inspect".
`existsSync` collapses EACCES, EIO and ELOOP to `false`, which could force a
removal after a transient error. I used explicit `lstat`/`realpath` presence
states and separated an absent blob from an unreadable one using `ls-tree` then
`cat-file`. Unreadable close-out records or a failed task index skip the whole
sweep.

No functional blocker remains. One handoff failed because the engineering
report exceeded the word cap; #1014 now counts only the engineer narrative, and
this draft is well inside it. A later handoff failed the docs build on a stale,
partially written `user-docs/.vitepress/dist/`; a clean rebuild regenerated the
missing raw `agent-skill.md` and the `user-docs-build` step now passes. Re-running
the changed suites locally on a loaded host passed all 89 tests across
`worktree-gc`, `status-command` and `support-bundle`, confirming the earlier
5-second timeouts were machine load, not a regression.

## Key learnings

A cleanup rule is safe only if it can name its evidence. Ancestry, byte
equality, and a content diff are evidence; status, archive flags, and path shape
are not. Fail-closed inspection matters as much as eligibility, because a
transient error that reads as "missing" is a data-loss path. One shared sweep
keeps the operator-facing counts honest, and the audit is part of the policy:
every retained entry records its commits, changed source paths, and dirt.
